newsitem.title: UK: MOTOR RACING-CUT PRICE FORMULA ONE REVS UP FOR FLOTATION.
newsitem.headline: MOTOR RACING-CUT PRICE FORMULA ONE REVS UP FOR FLOTATION.

text.p: Formula One motor racing is speeding for a flotation this summer -- although past value estimates of the business may be cut by as much as $1.0 billion, a source close to the deal said on Monday.

But Formula One's multi-millionaire owner and chief executive Bernie Ecclestone and U.S. investment bank Salomon Brothers are confounding talk that the deal was off or delayed partly because of rows with grand prix teams about their revenue share and their stake in the floated company.

Investment bankers say Formula One's coming to the market has been discussed for at least 6-12 months. The flotation of the business, which owns the intellectual property rights to Formula One international motor racing and controls television coverage, was initially estimated to be worth $3.5-4.0 billion.
But a source close to the complex deal, under which about 50 percent of the business might be floated in London around July, confirmed that estimates had been trimmed to a range of $2.5-$3.3 billion.

"The valuation is slightly lower than earlier expectations," the source said, but added: "We didn't know the structure of the deal." The source noted that because of the complexity of Formula One's businesses, timetables and figures were subject to change.

Further uncertainty was injected on Monday when the new British government's health secretary, Frank Dobson, said a ban on tobacco advertising proposed last week would extend to sports sponsorship. Draft legislation to ban tobacco advertising is expected by autumn.
British-based Formula One motor racing teams such as Williams, Benetton, Jordan, Tyrell and McLaren are among the most high-profile recipients of tobacco industry sponsorship.

Sources said it was likely Ecclestone would take a 30 percent stake in the floated group with both the FIA, the Paris-based world governing body of the sport, and the racing teams securing a 10 percent stake each.

The stock will effectively be classed as a media stock and is expected to sport the giddy price-earnings ratios of growth stocks. Television rights will be Formula One's main revenue driver, and valuations are based partly on expected earnings from pay-per-view TV.
At a presentation last Friday, syndicate banks were given forecasts for turnover of 200 million pounds this year, generating pre-tax profits of 85 million pounds.

But some analysts said the numbers looked optimistic because they were partly dependent on so far unproven new revenues from digital television. Investment bankers are also still grappling to make the figures add up.

"The actual corporate structures involved and the flow of economics around the different companies accruing from rights is slightly opaque and takes a bit of time to work your way through," noted one investment banker who has been following Salomon's progress on the flotation.
It also remains to be seen how the income from sponsors will be affected, who may be put off by restrictions on tobacco advertising and details of any compromise or transition period.
But Formula One and its new digital television network, FOCA TV, plans rewards from revolutionising the way subscibers view grand prix motor racing.

By investing in the latest digital telecommunications technology and offering subscribers up to six menu options operated by TV remote control for each grand prix, they want to ensure a unique vantage point for each armchair enthusiast.
Viewers can choose to sit in their favourite car during the race. Each F1 car will also be equipped with an on-board "black box" which monitors cornering and braking forces.

The central FOCA TV computer will also guarantee that no dramatic moments will be missed, by switching to the cameras in the car closest to the action when a set of parameters inside the on-board black box are exceeded.
Formula One's high-profile management line-up includes chairman Helmut Werner, former head of Germany's Mercedes-Benz and deputy chief executive Marco Piccinini, former Ferrari team manager.

The finance director will be David Wilson, who comes with a background in accountants Ernst & Young and leisure group Ladbroke Group Plc. Non-executives include Rob Rowley, finance director of Reuters Holdings Plc, and Walter Thoma of Philip Morris.
